summary: A country on the Atlantic coast of West Africa whose capital, Freetown, was founded by British abolitionists in the late 18th century to resettle freed slaves; it is known for its diamond resources and its civil war history.

ranking.name: Islam (Sunni)
ranking.description: Islam was introduced in the 18th century by Fulani and Mandinka traders and scholars from the north, and after the Islamic state of Futa Jallon (in present-day Guinea) was founded in 1727, Islam spread south with trade and jihad to northern Sierra Leone. During British colonial rule in the 19th century Islam continued to expand among the peoples of the interior, because unlike Christianity it was not tied to the colonizers. Today Muslims make up about three quarters, spread across the country and especially concentrated in the Temne and Limba areas of the north.

ranking.name: Christianity
ranking.description: Christianity was introduced in 1787 with the 'Province of Freedom' established at Freetown by British abolitionists, and in 1792 Black settlers from Nova Scotia brought Methodism and the Baptist church. Fourah Bay College, founded in 1827 by the Church Missionary Society, was the first Western-style university in West Africa and trained large numbers of African missionaries and intellectuals. Christians are concentrated in Freetown and the south and east, and are mainly Krio and Mende. Sierra Leone is known for Muslims and Christians living together in peace and intermarrying.

ranking.name: Traditional beliefs
ranking.description: Before Islam and Christianity became widespread, each of Sierra Leone's peoples had traditional beliefs, and the Mende 'Sande' women's secret society and 'Poro' men's secret society were responsible for initiation rites and social education. Because Islamization and Christianization are more than two hundred years old, few people follow purely traditional religion, but the tradition of the secret societies still exists widely, and many Muslims and Christians take part in them as well.

religion.background: The peoples of Sierra Leone originally believed in ancestral spirits and nature spirits, and secret societies played an important role in society. In the 18th century Islam came from the north, and in 1787 British abolitionists established a settlement for freed slaves at Freetown, bringing Christianity. In 1808 Freetown became a British colony, and in 1896 the interior became a protectorate. After independence Muslims and Christians lived together in peace, and even during the civil war of 1991–2002 religion was not a main cause of the conflict.

ranking.name: Mende
ranking.description: Mende belongs to the Mande branch of the Niger–Congo family and is the language of the Mende of the south and east, one of the most populous peoples of Sierra Leone. Mende is the regional lingua franca of the south and east, and in 1921 the Mende man Kisimi Kamara even created the Mende script. Because it stands in rivalry with the northern Temne language, politics after independence has also often run along the north–south ethnic divide.

ranking.name: Krio
ranking.description: Krio is an English-based creole that originated with the freed slaves who settled in Freetown after 1787, who came from Britain, Nova Scotia, Jamaica and also Africans rescued by the Royal Navy from slave ships. Krio is the mother tongue of the Krio people and the most widespread common language among the country's various groups, and more than ninety percent of the population can use Krio.

ranking.name: English
ranking.description: English was the language of administration and education during British colonial rule from 1808 and, after independence in 1961, continued as the official language, used in government, law, school education and the media. However, very few people speak English as a mother tongue, and most use Krio or their own ethnic languages in daily life.

language.history: Sierra Leone has more than twenty indigenous languages, belonging mainly to the Mande and Atlantic branches. In the 15th century Portuguese navigators named it 'Serra Leoa' (Lion Mountains), and Portuguese left some vocabulary along the coast. After 1787 the community of freed slaves in Freetown developed Krio, and after British colonization in 1808 English became the official language. After independence English remains the official language, and Krio is the de facto national lingua franca.

ranking.name: Cassava leaves (plasas)
ranking.description: Cassava leaves are pounded or finely chopped and stewed with palm oil, onions, chili and peanut butter, with chicken, beef or smoked fish added, with a rich flavor, and eaten with white rice.
ranking.history: Cassava originated in South America and was introduced to West Africa by the Portuguese after the 16th century, becoming an important crop in Sierra Leone, where people eat not only the root but also use the leaves as a main vegetable. Palm oil is a specialty of the West African rainforest and was an important export of Sierra Leone in the 19th century. Cassava leaves is regarded as Sierra Leone's national dish, and is indispensable at Sunday family lunches and important gatherings.

ranking.name: Jollof rice
ranking.description: Rice is cooked together with tomato, onion, bell pepper and spices, with chicken or beef added, cooked into red rice, often served with fried plantain and salad.
ranking.history: The name jollof comes from the Wolof (Jolof) Empire of Senegal in the 14th to 16th centuries, and this one-pot rice dish spread along the West African coast. Rice-growing in Sierra Leone has a long history, and African rice native to West Africa has been grown there for thousands of years. Jollof rice is the most common banquet staple at weddings, birthday parties and festivals.

ranking.name: Pepper soup
ranking.description: A clear soup simmered from chili, onion, spices and fish, chicken or goat meat, with a fierce heat and a rich aroma, often drunk as an appetizer or as a hangover remedy.
ranking.history: Pepper soup is a common soup throughout West Africa, with spices including the local grains of paradise; grains of paradise were once an important export spice of West Africa, and in the 15th century Europeans even called the coast near present-day Liberia the 'Pepper Coast'. In Sierra Leone, pepper soup is thought to drive out the cold and treat colds, is especially popular in the rainy season, and is often served in bars and at gatherings.

ranking.name: Akara (bean fritters)
ranking.description: Peeled black-eyed peas are soaked and ground into a puree, mixed with onion, chili and salt, scooped with a spoon into small balls and deep-fried, crisp outside and soft inside, often eaten for breakfast or as a snack.
ranking.history: Akara derives from the Yoruba 'akara' of Nigeria; in the 19th century Yoruba people rescued by the British Navy from slave ships settled in Freetown and brought this dish to Sierra Leone, where it became part of Krio cuisine. In Krio tradition, akara is distributed to guests at baby naming ceremonies, weddings and memorial services.

ranking.name: Fufu
ranking.description: Cassava is fermented and cooked, then pounded into a smooth, elastic dough, a small piece of which is pinched off by hand and dipped in soup or stew, with a slightly sour fermented flavor.
ranking.history: Fufu is a staple shared by West and Central Africa, and in Sierra Leone it is most commonly made from fermented cassava. Cassava was introduced from the Americas by the Portuguese after the 16th century and replaced some native crops. Making fufu requires long pounding, traditionally done together by the women of the household, and it is often served with okra soup, peanut soup or pepper soup.
